questions.prompt: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow inland waters, turn up in both South America and southern Africa, an ocean apart. What can these matching fossils suggest?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in shallow inland waters such as lagoons, are found in both South America and southern Africa, which are an ocean apart. What can these matching fossils suggest?

choices.text: The continents were once joined, especially if other evidence agrees
choices.rationale: Correct. A small shallow-water reptile that could not cross an ocean, found on both sides of one, points to land that was once connected. The fossils are one clue; matching rock layers and continental edges make the case much stronger.

choices.text: Mesosaurus swam across the open Atlantic Ocean to get there
choices.rationale: A small reptile of shallow inland waters could not survive a swim across thousands of kilometers of open ocean. That is exactly why its fossils are such a useful clue.

choices.text: The same reptile evolved separately, in identical form, on each continent
choices.rationale: One species appearing independently, identical in every way, on two continents is far less likely than one population living on land that was once joined.

choices.text: The fossils alone prove the continents were joined, so no other clues are needed
choices.rationale: One kind of clue can suggest a connection but cannot prove it alone. Fossils, matching rocks and continental edges together made a strong case, but most scientists accepted moving continents only after seafloor evidence showed how they could move.

questions.explanation: Matching fossils of an animal that could not cross an ocean suggest the lands where they lie were once connected. On its own, a fossil match is a clue rather than proof. The case grew stronger when it lined up with matching rock layers, mountain ranges and continental edges, and most scientists accepted it only when seafloor evidence showed how continents could move.
questions.misconception: Matching fossils prove a connection all by themselves, or the animals simply crossed the ocean.
questions.hint: Think about where a small reptile of shallow inland waters could and could not travel.

choices.text: The lands were once joined, and Antarctica was once much less icy
choices.rationale: Correct. One plant group spread across lands now split by oceans fits a single joined landmass, and fossil forests show Antarctica's climate was once far milder than today's ice sheet.

choices.text: Its seeds drifted across several oceans and sprouted on each shore

choices.text: Antarctica has always been as icy as it is today

choices.text: The lands were once joined, with Antarctica near the equator

questions.explanation: Glossopteris fossils form one connected pattern when the southern continents are fitted together, which supports a joined landmass. questions.misconception: Fossils of a plant in a cold place prove the land was once at the equator, or plants simply spread their seeds across oceans.
questions.hint: Ask two questions: how could one plant group reach all five places, and what do the tree rings say about where it grew?

questions.prompt: The Appalachian Mountains in North America and the Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa contain the same kinds of rock, of the same ages, stacked in the same order. What does this suggest?
questions.accessiblePrompt: The Appalachian Mountains in North America and the Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa are an ocean apart. They contain the same kinds of rock, the rocks are the same ages, and the layers are stacked in the same order. What does this suggest?

choices.text: They were once one mountain range that later split apart
choices.rationale: Correct. Identical rock types, ages and layer order on two coasts fit one range that was torn apart as the continents separated.

choices.text: Every mountain range on Earth has these same rock layers
choices.rationale: Mountain ranges differ a lot in their rocks and ages. This match is unusual, which is why it counts as evidence.

choices.text: The two ranges formed separately in similar settings, so they only look alike
choices.rationale: Similar settings can make similar kinds of rock, but not the same rock ages stacked in the same order on two coasts. One range torn in two explains all three matches.

choices.text: The match is a coincidence that says nothing about the continents' past
choices.rationale: Matching rock types, rock ages and layer order all at once would be extremely unlikely to happen by chance in two unrelated places, which is why geologists treat the match as evidence.

questions.explanation: When rock types, ages and the order of layers all match across an ocean, the simplest explanation is that the rocks formed together in one place. Wegener used this match as evidence that North America and Africa once sat side by side, with the range split as the continents moved apart.
questions.misconception: Similar rocks on continents far apart are just a coincidence.
questions.hint: Two separate ranges might share one feature by chance. How likely is it that rock type, age and layer order would all match?

questions.prompt: Continental drift began as a hypothesis in 1912. Plate tectonics became a scientific theory in the 1960s. Which statement best describes that change?

choices.text: It gained a mechanism and wide evidence but stays open to revision
choices.rationale: Correct. A theory is backed by a large body of evidence and explains many observations, including how plates move. Scientists still refine details, such as which forces matter most.

choices.text: It was proven for all time, so scientists may never revise it again
choices.rationale: Even strong theories stay open to new evidence. Scientists still debate parts of plate tectonics, such as the exact mix of driving forces.

choices.text: Theory means a guess, so it is no more certain than the old hypothesis
choices.rationale: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation supported by lots of evidence, not a hunch.

choices.text: Scientists simply renamed the old idea without adding any new evidence

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable idea based on limited evidence. A scientific theory pulls together a large body of evidence and explains many observations: plate tectonics explains why continents moved, why seafloor ages form a pattern and where earthquakes cluster. Like all science, it stays open to revision if new evidence calls for it.
questions.misconception: A theory is either an unproven guess or a final fact that can never change.
questions.hint: Think about what new evidence and explanations were added between 1912 and the 1960s, and whether science ever closes the door on new evidence.

items.text: The cool, rigid top layer of the mantle
items.rationale: Lithosphere: the surprise member. The lithosphere is the crust plus the stiff uppermost part of the mantle.

questions.explanation: The lithosphere is defined by stiffness, not by a single layer name. It includes all of the crust plus the cool, rigid top of the mantle. Beneath it, hotter mantle rock can slowly flow, which is why the rigid lithosphere can move as plates.

questions.prompt: How did scientists discover that the top of Earth's mantle is rigid, while hotter mantle rock below it can slowly flow?
questions.accessiblePrompt: How did scientists discover that the top of Earth's mantle is rigid, while hotter mantle rock below it can slowly flow?

choices.text: By tracking how earthquake waves change speed and direction inside Earth
choices.rationale: Correct. Seismographs around the world record earthquake waves, and changes in the waves' speed and path reveal layers with different properties.

choices.text: By drilling through the crust and pulling up samples of the mantle
choices.rationale: No drill has gone all the way through the crust into the mantle; the deepest hole drilled down from the surface is about 12 kilometers. Mantle rock has been drilled only where it lies exposed on the seafloor, long after the layers were mapped.

choices.text: By lowering thermometers down volcanoes into the mantle
choices.rationale: No instrument can be lowered through a volcano into the mantle; the evidence comes from waves passing through rock.

choices.text: By studying lava, which pours up from a liquid layer just under the crust
choices.rationale: There is no worldwide liquid layer just under the crust. Lava comes from rock that melts only in certain places, so it cannot show which parts of the mantle are rigid and which slowly flow.

questions.explanation: Scientists cannot visit the mantle, so they read it from earthquake waves. The waves speed up, slow down and bend as they pass into rock with different properties. Mapping those changes revealed a cool, rigid outer shell above hotter rock that can slowly flow. No drill has gone all the way through the crust into the mantle; the deepest hole drilled from the surface reaches only about 12 km.
questions.misconception: Scientists know what Earth's interior is like because they have drilled through it, seen it directly or sampled a liquid layer beneath the crust.
questions.hint: No one can travel to the mantle or see it. What can pass through solid rock and be recorded back at the surface?

evidence.locator: Section 2. Discovering Earth's Interior and Figure 2

questions.prompt: Along most of the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific and North American plates move past each other in sudden jerks that cause earthquakes, rather than sliding smoothly. Why?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Along most of the San Andreas Fault in California, the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate move past each other in sudden jerks that cause earthquakes, rather than sliding smoothly. Why?

choices.text: The plates stick, stress builds up, then the rock slips all at once
choices.rationale: Correct. Friction locks the plates while they keep being pushed; once the stress is more than the rock can hold, the rock lurches and the stored energy is released as an earthquake.

choices.text: Magma explodes upward wherever the two plates touch
choices.rationale: Transform boundaries are known for earthquakes from slipping rock, not for magma bursting out.

choices.text: One plate dives under the other and scrapes the bottom
choices.rationale: That is subduction at a convergent boundary. At a transform boundary the plates move sideways and neither one sinks.

choices.text: The plates move a few centimeters each day, too fast to slide calmly
choices.rationale: Plates move only centimeters per year; the shaking comes from stored stress being released, not from high speed.

questions.limitations: Knowing how stress builds helps scientists estimate long-term earthquake risk; it does not predict the exact time of an earthquake. One central stretch of the San Andreas creeps fairly steadily with only small quakes; this question is about the locked stretches, which store stress and release it in earthquakes (L16-RF19). Averaged over many years, USGS measures these plates moving past each other about 5 cm (50 mm) a year; the textbook's 5 mm looks like a units slip (L16-RF1).
questions.explanation: Along locked stretches, transform motion is jerky: the rocks catch on each other while the plates keep pushing, so stress builds for years. When it exceeds what the rock can hold, the rock slips suddenly and causes an earthquake.
questions.misconception: Earthquakes at a transform boundary come from magma or from one plate diving under the other, rather than from stress that builds and is suddenly released.
questions.hint: Imagine pressing two rough blocks together and pushing them past each other. Is the motion smooth?

questions.prompt: Mesosaurus fossils are found in South America and southern Africa. Fossils of Lystrosaurus, a land animal, are found in southern Africa, India and Antarctica. Neither animal could cross an open ocean. Which reconstructed map fits both clues?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Here are two fossil clues. First, Mesosaurus fossils are found in South America and southern Africa. Second, fossils of Lystrosaurus, an animal that lived on land, are found in southern Africa, India and Antarctica. Neither animal could cross an open ocean. Which reconstructed map of these four lands fits both clues?

choices.text: Africa at the center, joined to South America and to India and Antarctica
choices.rationale: Correct. Mesosaurus needs South America and Africa joined, and Lystrosaurus needs Africa, India and Antarctica joined. Of these maps, only this one gives both animals a land path.

choices.text: South America beside Africa, with India and Antarctica far off across open ocean
choices.rationale: Fits Mesosaurus, but leaves Lystrosaurus with no land path from Africa to India and Antarctica.

choices.text: Africa beside India and Antarctica, with South America far off across open ocean
choices.rationale: Fits Lystrosaurus, but strands Mesosaurus on two shores of an ocean it could not cross.

choices.text: All four lands far apart across open ocean, just as they are today
choices.rationale: Fits neither clue: both animals would have had to cross oceans.

questions.limitations: Lystrosaurus fossils have also been found in parts of Asia, such as China and Russia, so the textbook's word "only" is not repeated; the item uses the southern lands shown on the textbook's map (L16-RF15). The maps are simplified sketches; real reconstructions also use rock and shelf matches.
questions.explanation: Each fossil links only some of the lands, so you need both clues. Mesosaurus ties South America to Africa, and Lystrosaurus ties Africa to India and Antarctica, so all four lands must once have been joined. With rock and shelf matches as well, scientists place Africa beside South America on one side and beside India and Antarctica on the other, as part of Pangaea.
questions.misconception: Each fossil clue can be read alone; you never need to combine clues to rebuild the old map.
questions.hint: Test each map against each animal: does every animal have a land path between all the places it is found?

evidence.locator: Section 1. Wegener's Hypothesis, Evidence for Continental Drift and Figure 1B
evidence.supports: Mesosaurus fossils occur in South America and Africa, and Lystrosaurus, a plant eater that lived on land, has fossils in Antarctica, southeastern Africa and India; neither animal could have crossed the ocean between them.

evidence.supports: The map shows Mesosaurus fossils in South America and southern Africa, and Lystrosaurus fossils in southern Africa, India and Antarctica.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of kilometers below the surface, mantle rock slowly circulates in loops called convection cells. What supplies the energy that keeps this circulation going?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Hundreds of kilometers below the surface, mantle rock slowly circulates in loops called convection cells. What supplies the energy that keeps this circulation going?

choices.text: Heat flowing out from Earth's hot interior
choices.rationale: Correct. Rock warmed from below expands, becomes less dense and slowly rises, while cooled rock sinks; the heat comes from deep inside Earth.

choices.text: Sunlight warming the land and the oceans
choices.rationale: Sunlight warms only Earth's surface; it cannot reach rock hundreds of kilometers down.

choices.text: Earthquakes shaking the mantle rock loose
choices.rationale: This reverses cause and effect: earthquakes happen because plates move; they do not power the mantle's flow.

choices.text: Ocean currents dragging the rock along beneath them
choices.rationale: Currents move water, not rock deep in the mantle; the seafloor moves because the plate it belongs to moves.

questions.limitations: Convection is one part of a linked system; scientists still debate how much it, compared with the pull of sinking plates, drives plate motion (L16-RF6).
questions.explanation: Convection needs heat from below. Earth's interior is hot, so mantle rock warmed from below expands, becomes less dense and slowly rises, while rock that has cooled grows denser and sinks, all while staying mostly solid. Sunlight warms only the surface and cannot reach the deep mantle.
questions.misconception: The Sun, earthquakes or ocean currents power the slow motion deep inside Earth.
questions.hint: A pot of soup circulates when the stove heats it from below. What plays the stove's role for the mantle?

evidence.locator: Section 6, Three Processes That Drive Plate Motion and Figure 6B
evidence.supports: Energy in Earth's interior makes mantle rock move slowly in convection cells: heated rock expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooled rock contracts, becomes denser and sinks.

evidence.title: Mantle
evidence.supports: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can move plastically over millions of years.

evidence.title: Some unanswered questions (This Dynamic Earth)
evidence.supports: Slab pull is now considered the main driving force of plate tectonics, and none of the proposed mechanisms can explain all facets of plate movement.

questions.prompt: Put these steps toward the theory of plate tectonics in the order they happened.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put five steps toward the theory of plate tectonics in order, from earliest to latest. The steps are: ships use sound echoes to map the shape of the seafloor; a mapmaker notices that the coasts on both sides of the Atlantic could fit together; drill cores show seafloor rock getting older with distance from the ridge; Wegener proposes that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart; scientists propose that new seafloor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward.

items.text: Ships use sound echoes to map the shape of the seafloor
items.rationale: Third: ships were mapping the seafloor with sound echoes by the 1920s, after Wegener's proposal. The ridges and trenches they revealed later needed an explanation.

items.text: A mapmaker notices that the coasts on both sides of the Atlantic could fit together
items.rationale: First: Abraham Ortelius noticed the fit in 1596, centuries before anyone could explain it.

items.text: Drill cores show seafloor rock getting older with distance from the ridge
items.rationale: Last: in 1968 the Glomar Challenger's cores tested seafloor spreading and supported it. A test has to come after the idea it tests.

items.text: Wegener proposes that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart
items.rationale: Second: Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, using fossil and rock clues found on land.

items.text: Scientists propose that new seafloor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward
items.rationale: Fourth: seafloor spreading was proposed in the early 1960s to explain the seafloor features that sound mapping had revealed.

questions.explanation: The theory was built step by step. A mapmaker's observation (1596) was taken up in Wegener's hypothesis (1912); new technology revealed the seafloor (from the 1920s); a new idea explained what it showed (early 1960s); and drilling tested that idea's prediction (1968). Each step built on the ones before it.
questions.misconception: A scientific theory appears all at once, rather than being built from observations, hypotheses, new tools and tests over time.
questions.hint: A test must come after the idea it tests, and an idea about the seafloor needs someone to have mapped the seafloor first.

evidence.locator: Section 1. Wegener's Hypothesis
evidence.supports: Abraham Ortelius noticed in 1596 that the continents around the Atlantic looked as if they could fit together; Wegener reintroduced the idea of a former supercontinent in 1912.

evidence.locator: Section 4. Discovering Features of the Seafloor
evidence.supports: By the 1920s, scientists were using sound waves to map seafloor features; sonar later revealed the mid-ocean ridge, fracture zones, trenches and continental shelves.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Seafloor Spreading
evidence.supports: In the early 1960s, scientists hypothesized that new lithosphere continuously forms at the mid-ocean ridge, a process later called seafloor spreading.

evidence.locator: Section 5, Testing for Seafloor Spreading
evidence.supports: In 1968 the Glomar Challenger collected seafloor samples on both sides of the ridge, and the data showed oceanic crust getting older with distance from the ridge, supporting seafloor spreading.

evidence.locator: Section 6, From Hypothesis to Theory
evidence.supports: Wegener proposed the continental drift hypothesis in 1912, and scientists developed the theory of plate tectonics in the 1960s.

questions.prompt: Two plates are pulling apart beneath a sea. If they keep moving this way, what will happen there over time?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Two tectonic plates are pulling apart from each other beneath a sea. If they keep moving this way, what will happen there over time?

choices.text: New lithosphere forms between them and the sea widens
choices.rationale: Correct. As the plates separate, magma rises into the gap and cools into new lithosphere, so the sea between them slowly grows wider, as the Red Sea is doing.

choices.text: One plate sinks beneath the other, and a deep trench forms
choices.rationale: That happens where plates move toward each other, at a convergent boundary such as the one off South America.

choices.text: The plates lock, then lurch sideways past each other
choices.rationale: Sticking and then slipping sideways is transform motion, as along the San Andreas Fault; these plates are moving apart instead.

choices.text: The sea slowly narrows until the two shores finally meet
choices.rationale: That is the reverse of what happens: plates moving apart open space between them, so the sea gets wider, not narrower.

questions.explanation: Plates moving apart leave a gap that rising magma fills. The magma cools into new lithosphere, so the sea between the plates grows wider over time. The Red Sea between the African and Arabian plates is widening this way, and seafloor spreading of the same kind moved South America and Africa apart as the Atlantic opened.
questions.misconception: Every plate boundary makes a trench, or plates moving apart close up the sea between them.
questions.hint: Picture two plates moving away from each other. What has to fill the space between them?

evidence.locator: Section 7. Tracking Plate Motion, Divergent Motion and Figure 7
evidence.supports: As two plates diverge, magma rises between them and cools to form new lithosphere; this seafloor spreading makes oceans and seas wider, as the African and Arabian plates widen the Red Sea.

evidence.locator: Section 4, Seafloor Spreading
evidence.supports: Seafloor spreading helped explain how South America and Africa moved away from each other.
